newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul says N.Korea nuclear project "back on track".
newsitem.headline: Seoul says N.Korea nuclear project "back on track".

text.p: A landmark nuclear pact with North Korea will be resuscitated next week in the first concrete step to repair the political damage from September's incursion of a North Korean submarine, Seoul officials said on Friday.
South Korea's Deputy Prime Minister Kwon O-kie said two protocols would be signed next week between a U.S.-led consortium and Pyongyang for building light-water reactors.
Kwon told government and ruling party officials that he hoped an apology by Pyongyang on Sunday over the submarine incursion into the South would help lead to better inter-Korean relations.
"This incident taught North Korea that provocation has always had its price," Kwon's spokesman quoted him as saying.
Kwon said he believed the communist North had to take steps to leave the incident behind as it sought aid to handle a severe food shortage and hopes to end its diplomatic isolation.
"North Korea must have realised that nothing is possible after aggravating South-North relations," he was quoted as saying.

The incursion froze all contacts between the two Koreas. South Korea is largely financing the reactors promised to North Korea in a 1994 agreement with the United States that halted Pyongyang's suspected nuclear weapons programme.

Seoul officials said the protocols to be signed by the Korean Peninsula Energy Development Organisation (KEDO) and Pyongyang would set the site for the reactors and specify services to be provided by North Korea for the project.
"It is the first step to put the nuclear project back on track since the submarine incident," a KEDO official said.
KEDO and North Korea have agreed in principle to build the reactors in Sinpo, about 150 miles (240 km) northeast of Pyongyang.
The nuclear pact was signed after three years of difficult talks on replacing communist North Korea's nuclear programme with one that produced less weapons-grade plutonium.
Light water reactors are less suited to making plutonium for weapons, which Washington and its allies suspected North Korea was doing with its Soviet-model plants.

Last year, KEDO and North Korea signed three protocol agreements covering transportation and communication matters related to construction of the reactors as well as what privileges will be granted to officials and workers visiting the North for the project.

"With the two protocols to be signed next week, all basic framework would have been laid out for the start of the construction," the KEDO official said. "But preparations for the construction would take several more months."
After Pyongyang made its apology, U.S. and South Korean officials said they were working out details of a briefing on four-nation peace talks that Pyongyang agreed to attend.
Kwon said on Friday he expected a briefing on the peace talks late in January. The talks, jointly proposed by the United States and South Korea, would also include China.
U.S. officials have also said in Washington that they are considering providing more food aid to stave off looming famine in North Korea.
Cargill, the world's largest grain trading company, was awaiting U.S. Treasury Department approval to barter up to two million tonnes of grain to famine-striken North Korea.
U.S. officials said they were considering easing trade sanctions against North Korea to allow barter deals.
